FOR INDEPENDENT ROLL-OFF DUMPSTER RENTAL OPERATORS

The scale ticket decides your margin, not the rental price.

A rental quote covers an included weight allowance, but disposal is billed by the ton at the transfer station once the container actually comes back — and the customer's fill, not you, decides what it weighs. This free calculator prices a rental from that allowance, then checks whether your overage rate even covers what an extra ton costs you, and lets you plug in the real scale ticket once you have it.

Private by default

Everything on this page runs in your browser. Your job details, prices, and scale tickets are never uploaded, there is no account, and nothing is saved when you close the tab. We count only anonymous local feature events (quote-priced, weight-ticket-checked) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no job details, prices, or weights are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Common questions

Why does the calculator price the rental at the included weight allowance instead of the weight I expect the job to hit?

Because that is what the rental agreement actually promises: a price for up to the allowance, with anything over billed separately as overage. Pricing the base rental from your expected weight instead would double-count the disposal cost for tons that are supposed to be billed as overage, not baked into the sticker price.

What happens if my overage rate is lower than my tipping fee?

Every ton over the allowance then costs you more to dispose of than you charge the customer for it, so the fee meant to protect your margin instead erodes it — and the loss has no ceiling as the load gets heavier. The calculator flags this directly and reports how many overage tons would erase the rental's entire built-in profit.

Why show extra rental days as pure revenue with no added cost?

Because in this model a container sitting on a job site longer does not add disposal weight, labor, or mileage by itself — those are billed when the container is actually hauled. If your business does incur a real cost for a container sitting longer (a second unit tied up, a rental yard fee), fold that into the flat other-cost field.

Does anything about my costs or a customer's scale ticket get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and nothing you type is saved anywhere — it exists only in the page while it is open. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Dumpster Rental Margin Calculator

Dumpster rental margin calculator vs a spreadsheet

A pricing spreadsheet can get one job's numbers right if every cell is filled in correctly. What it can't do on its own is answer the question that actually protects your margin over time: is the overage rate on your rate card, by itself, priced above what an extra ton costs you to dispose of? That's a two-number comparison independent of any specific job, and most per-job sheets have no cell for it.

What a per-job spreadsheet tracks, and what it doesn't

A per-job pricing spreadsheetThis calculator
Base rental vs. overageUsually one price cell for the job totalPrices the base rental from the included weight allowance only, then computes overage separately
Overage rate vs. tipping feeNot compared automatically — both are just cost/revenue inputs on the same rowFlags an overage rate below the tipping fee directly, and reports how many overage tons would erase the job's profit
Labor, mileage, equipmentOften one blended "average cost per haul" figureItemized: driver hours and rate, round-trip miles and mileage rate, equipment cost, separate from disposal
Scale ticket reconciliationA separate one-off worksheet, easy to skip on a busy dayBuilt into the same page — enter the actual weight to check it against this same quote's breakeven

One rate card, two outcomes

Take a rate card with a $65/ton tipping fee and a $55/ton overage rate — a common drift when the overage line was set once and the transfer station has raised its tipping fee since. Priced at the calculator's own default allowance and cost inputs, the base rental (2 tons included, 30% target margin) comes out to $351.01 and clears $105.30 in built-in profit. Nothing on that job's own spreadsheet row looks wrong, because a rental that stays inside its allowance never touches the overage rate at all.

The first heavy job changes that. A shingle tear-off in the same 20-yard container that actually weighs 5 tons runs 3 tons over the allowance:

Overage revenue (3 tons × $55/ton charged)$165.00
Overage disposal cost (3 tons × $65/ton tipping fee)$195.00
Loss on the overage tons alone−$30.00
Job profit including the base rental's margin$75.30 (down from $105.30 if the job had stayed at allowance)
Overage tons this job could absorb before flipping to a net loss10.53 tons

The job as a whole still turns a profit, which is exactly why a spreadsheet totaling one number per job reads it as a normal day. The $30 lost on the overage tons is real and it recurs on every heavy job this rate card prices, but it never appears as its own line unless the overage rate and the tipping fee are kept apart on purpose and checked against each other — a structural comparison a per-job total, by design, doesn't make.

Why "tons before loss" needs two separate numbers

The 10.53-ton figure above — how many overage tons this specific job could take before its entire built-in profit is gone — only exists because the tipping fee and the overage rate are held apart as two distinct inputs, then divided into the base rental's profit. A spreadsheet that totals revenue minus cost for the job as one number never produces that figure, because by the time the total is computed, the two rates that would have to be compared have already been folded together. Recomputing it by hand for every rate change is the reason this one check is what the calculator adds over a general-purpose sheet, not the arithmetic underneath it.

Open the Dumpster Rental Margin Calculator to check your own overage rate against your own tipping fee, or read why your overage fee might be losing you money for the method behind it. Already comparing this against a field-service platform? See this calculator vs Jobber.

Common questions

What does a per-job pricing spreadsheet usually get right, and what does it miss?

Filled in carefully, a spreadsheet can get one job's own revenue and cost right — rental price plus overage charged, minus disposal, labor, mileage and equipment for that job. What it doesn't do on its own is check whether your overage rate, by itself, is priced above what an extra ton actually costs you at the transfer station. That is a comparison between two rate-card numbers, independent of any single job, and a per-job total has no cell for it unless someone builds one specifically.

Why can an underpriced overage rate look fine for months and then lose money on one job?

Because most jobs never test it. A rental that stays inside its included weight allowance never charges overage at all, so a rate card can carry an overage fee below the tipping fee indefinitely with nothing on any routine job's spreadsheet row to reveal it. The gap only shows up on a job heavy enough to exceed the allowance — a shingle tear-off, a concrete tear-out, wet dirt — and by then it is being charged, not caught.

What is "tons before loss," and why can't a flat per-job total compute it?

It is how many overage tons a specific job can absorb before the rate's own per-ton loss erases that job's entire built-in profit. Computing it needs the tipping fee and the overage rate held apart as two separate figures, divided into the base rental's profit — a spreadsheet that only ever totals one blended number per job has nothing to divide, because the two rates were never kept separate in the first place.

Does this calculator store or upload anything I type?

No. Every field runs in your browser and nothing survives closing the tab. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off from the calculator page.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is an account-based platform for running a service company's whole operation, including scheduling a drop-off or pickup and invoicing the customer once a rental is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this roll-off rental cost, given its included weight allowance, tipping fee and overage rate, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is a field service management platform used by home and trade service businesses — lawn care, cleaning, HVAC, plumbing, junk removal and general contracting among them — to run client management and online quoting, scheduling and crew or driver dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client-facing hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Jobber's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of field service software describe scheduling a job, dispatching a driver, and invoicing and collecting payment once a price already exists; none describe working out whether a container's overage rate actually covers what an extra ton of disposal costs, or reconciling a rental's price against the scale ticket that comes back once the job is done — which is what this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage a customer list, schedule a driver's route, or collect a payment. It takes a container size, the included weight allowance and rental days, the tipping fee you pay and the overage rate you charge, driver labor, round-trip mileage, a flat dump/gate fee, equipment cost, overhead and target margin, and turns that into the rental price, the breakeven at the allowance, and the profit if the job goes as expected — plus, once the container is back and weighed, a check of the real scale ticket against that same breakeven, so an overage rate priced below the tipping fee shows up as a loss before it repeats across a fleet of containers. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it

Most roll-off operators get different value from each: Jobber (or a comparable field service platform) for managing customers, scheduling drivers and collecting payment across an ongoing business as an account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one rental should cost from its weight allowance and overage rate before it is quoted, and whether a real scale ticket still clears the breakeven once the job is done. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a scheduled job, an invoice, or a signed rental agreement.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Jobber?

They do different jobs, and a roll-off dumpster rental operator of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. Jobber is a field service management platform used across home and trade service businesses — including hauling and waste-adjacent trades — to run client management and quoting, scheduling and dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. This calculator does one narrower thing: it takes a rental's included weight allowance, tipping fee, overage rate, rental days, driver labor, mileage and equipment cost, and turns that into the rental price, the breakeven at the allowance, and — once a scale ticket comes back — the real profit and margin the job actually left. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. An operator already scheduling drop-offs and pickups, invoicing customers, and taking payments across a fleet of containers is better served by Jobber or a comparable field service platform; an operator who wants an instant, private answer to what one rental should cost before it is quoted, and whether the overage rate even covers the tipping fee, is in the right place here.

why-your-overage-fee-might-be-losing-you.text:
← Dumpster rental margin calculator

Why your overage fee might be losing you money

An overage rate looks like it protects your margin: the customer fills the container past the included allowance, you charge them a per-ton fee for the extra weight. But that fee only protects anything if it is priced above what disposal actually costs you. Set it below your own tipping fee, and every ton over the allowance loses money — on the exact jobs, heavy tear-offs and demo debris, where the most overage tons pile up.

Open the free dumpster rental calculator

Why this is easy to get wrong

The base rental price hides it. A well-priced base rental — say $351 for a 20-yard container with a 2-ton allowance, 7 days, and a healthy 30% target margin — looks perfectly profitable on paper. That price only has to cover disposal up to the allowance; it says nothing about whether the overage rate is safe.

Overage rates often get set by "what competitors charge," not by cost. A round number like $50/ton looks reasonable next to a $65/ton tipping fee, until you notice it's below the tipping fee, not above it — the fee is already losing $15 on every ton before your labor, mileage, or overhead are even counted.

The risk doesn't show up until the heavy job. A light cleanout that stays under the allowance never touches the overage rate at all. It's the shingle tear-off, the concrete tear-out, or the wet-dirt job — material that runs heavy for its volume — that pushes weight well past the allowance and turns a mispriced overage fee into a real loss.

Worked example

A container is rented at the price above: 20 yards, 2-ton allowance, 7 included days, a $65/ton tipping fee, driver labor and mileage totaling about $76, $20 equipment cost, 10% overhead, and a 30% target margin — quoting a base price of $351.01 with $105.30 of built-in profit. The overage rate is set at $50/ton, $15 below the tipping fee. A roofing tear-off comes back on the scale at 10 tons — 8 tons over the allowance:

FigureValue
Base rental price (covers the 2-ton allowance)$351.01
Overage billed (8 tons × $50)$400.00
Total revenue$751.01
Disposal cost (10 tons × $65 + $10 gate fee)$660.00
Labor, mileage, equipment & overhead$105.71
Total cost$765.71
Net profit−$14.70

A job that started with over $105 of built-in profit at the allowance ends up a small loss once the real weight ticket comes in — and it only takes about 7 overage tons for this specific rental's entire built-in profit to disappear (the calculator reports this number, maxOverageTonsBeforeLoss, for your own numbers). A heavier job than this one — a full container of shingles instead of mixed debris — would lose far more, because nothing about this overage rate has a floor.

Common questions

How do I know if my dumpster overage rate is priced correctly?

Compare it directly to your own tipping fee per ton, not to what competitors advertise. If your overage rate is lower than what the transfer station charges you per ton, every ton the customer goes over the included allowance costs you more to dispose of than you collect for it.

Why would a $351 rental job lose money?

Because the rental price only covers disposal up to the included weight allowance. A shingle tear-off or a concrete job can weigh far more than a light cleanout at the same container size, and if the overage rate charged for the extra tons is below the tipping fee, the loss on those tons can exceed the profit built into the base price.

Does raising the base rental price fix a mispriced overage rate?

Only up to a point. A higher base price gives the job more built-in profit to absorb losing overage tons before it goes negative, but the overage rate itself keeps losing money on every ton past that point — there is no ceiling on a heavy enough load. Fixing the overage rate itself, so it covers the tipping fee with room for margin, is the only fix that scales.

How do I estimate the weight before the job, to know if this risk applies?

By material, not container size: shingles, concrete, dirt, and brick run far heavier per yard than furniture, cardboard, or general household junk. A 20-yard container of shingles can weigh several times what the same container holds in light cleanout debris, which is why the same allowance and overage rate can be safe for one job type and a loss for another.
